title: Chip Export Controls Are Rewriting Hardware Plans
body:
## What's Happening With US Semiconductor Export Controls

The US government has taken another step to restrict the flow of advanced semiconductors to China, tightening an export control framework that has been building for several years. The latest actions reflect a continued policy position that high-performance chips represent a strategic national interest, not just a commercial commodity. [...] Escalating restrictions: The US government has moved to tighten semiconductor export controls targeting China, further limiting access to advanced chips used across industrial and commercial hardware applications.
 Broader hardware exposure: The restrictions extend beyond consumer electronics, with implications for robotics, autonomous systems, IoT sensors, and any physical automation technology that depends on high-performance chips. [...] Industry uncertainty: Leadership controversies in the semiconductor sector are compounding policy unpredictability, making long-term hardware procurement planning more difficult for operations teams.
 Dual-market pressure: Supply chain hardware manufacturers operating in both US and China-adjacent markets face increasing pressure to manage separate supply lines or redesign products around compliant chip architectures.

title: Agentic AI: Regulators respond to launch of first personal AI agents | TLT LLP
body:
# Agentic I: Regulators respond to launch of first personal AI agents

The UK launch of Meta's Muse tool – a personal AI agent that can send emails, book travel, and even do the Christmas shopping – has drawn a co-ordinated response from UK regulators. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and the Information Commission's Office (ICO) have each confirmed that they had been in talks with Meta ahead of the launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. [...] On Muse, the CMA noted that it engaged with Meta prior to the launch, following which Meta made amendments to its terms and conditions to make them fairer. The CMA will not be taking its eye off deployment of the tool, with Sarah Cardell, Chief Executive of the CMA, stating that: "We now need to examine carefully how Muse actually works in practice. We will be closely monitoring this and if we have concerns we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers." [...] The ICO made clear to Meta before launch that users and the wider public must be able to understand and control how Muse uses their personal data. Meta committed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme that will allow the ICO to review how Muse works in practice, how users experience it and what feedback they provide as the product develops.

title: What is agentic AI? Definition, how it works, and examples | Sierra
body:
- Takes only the actions the company allows, with limits on amounts and changes
- Verifies the customer's identity before it changes an account or booking
- Is tested on realistic conversations before launch and after every change
- Gives customers an easy way to reach a person if escalation is required

Companies use Sierra to build AI agents that can take action for customers over chat and voice. See how companies build on Sierra. [...] Generative AI creates content, such as text, images, or code, in response to a prompt. Asked about the cancelled flight, a generative AI tool can write a clear reply that explains the traveler's rebooking options. Agentic AI uses generative AI models to understand the traveler and reply in natural language, and then it acts: it checks the booking and makes the change. Most agentic AI systems are built on top of generative AI models. [...] "Agentic" describes how the AI behaves: it acts with some independence to reach a goal. The software that does this work is an AI agent, so agentic AI is the approach, and AI agents are what companies build with it.

## How does agentic AI work?

What makes AI agentic is that it chooses its next step based on what it has just learned. A scripted system runs the same steps every time. An agentic system starts from the goal, tries a step, looks at the result, and decides what to do next.

Equifax, 2017. On March 7, 2017 the Apache Software Foundation disclosed a critical flaw in its Struts web framework (CVE-2017-5638, CVSS 9.8) and released a fix the same day. The US government's computer emergency team issued an alert on March 8. According to the US House Oversight Committee's December 2018 report, Equifax ran a scan for the flaw that did not find it on its online dispute portal, and attackers got in through that portal on May 13, 2017. They stayed for 76 days before the [...] The most dangerous outcome is remote code execution: an attacker anywhere on the internet can make the vulnerable system run their commands, with no password. Log4Shell, the Apache Struts flaw behind the Equifax breach, and the Ivanti VPN flaws all allowed it, alone or chained together.

## CVE: a name for every flaw [...] The attackers lesson showed that exploiting a software vulnerability is now the most common first step in a breach: 31% of breaches in Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report and 32% of the intrusions in Mandiant's M-Trends 2026. The zero-day glossary entry covers flaws that attackers find before the vendor does. This lesson covers the far larger group that is already known, with a fix available, and still gets exploited because the fix has not been applied.

The hard tech underpinning AI is also mired in geopolitics. Leading chip-producing nations restrict which countries can buy certain chips, with export and import controls shifting frequently. The US, for example, has restricted sales of advanced chips to China to some extent since 2022, while China has barred foreign AI chips from state-funded data centers. Policies like these mean the chips companies can use in one region may be unacceptable in another. [...] - Which of our critical technologies (AI models, cloud, chips and devices, key software and data) depend on a single country, company or jurisdiction? And how could we diversify?
- How would we adapt — and how quickly — if a key AI model, service or component became unavailable overnight through export controls, sanctions, a vendor ban or retaliation? [...] ## Geopolitical risk affects the entire AI supply chain

Geopolitics does not just impact technology: it affects the entire AI supply chain, from the extent of a nation’s power generation infrastructure to the availability of skilled talent. And issues in any one sphere can have serious knock-on effects. For example, high demand for essential equipment for data centers is increasing lead times and prices for other buyers.
